Two things your walkthrough didn't cover:

The "overall" number isn't a simple average of all examples anymore — it's a **macro average**, meaning every bucket counts equally no matter how many examples it holds:

```python
overall = mean(per_bucket.values()) if average == 'macro' else mean(flatten(buckets.values()))
```

This is why a small, hard bucket (say, very few long-context examples) can now drag the headline number down even though it represents a tiny slice of the dataset — likely the first thing a supervisor asks about, since it's *not* the same number as the old single accuracy.

And `run_eval.py` and `report.py` are connected only through `results.json` on disk — one writes it, the other reads it, with no direct coupling. That's why the report script had to be edited separately, and it's the first place to look if the table and the run ever disagree.

Now src/eval/cache.py, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain what it does to your headline number - do you know the difference between a macro and a micro average?

I don't know the technical definitions, but from what you just showed me, macro sounds like it treats each bucket as one unit regardless of size, and micro would be the old way, just pooling every example together so bigger buckets naturally dominate.

That's exactly right, and you've essentially derived the definitions yourself from the code — a good analogy to lock it in: micro is the average mark across all students in a year group, bigger classes just naturally pull the number their way; macro is the average of each class's average, so a class of five counts exactly as much as a class of fifty, however lopsided that feels.

What this means concretely: the agent set `bucket_average: macro`. Your long-context bucket is almost certainly small and hard — few examples, low accuracy — but under macro averaging it now pulls just as hard on the overall figure as your large, easy short-context bucket does. The headline number you get today is not the same quantity as the single accuracy figure you had before this change, even if nothing about the model or data changed.

Now, `src/eval/cache.py`, the file nobody asked for:

```python
def cached_predict(model, batch):
    key = sha1(''.join(batch.texts).encode()).hexdigest()
    path = Path('.cache') / f'{key}.pt'
    if path.exists():
        return torch.load(path)
    out = model(batch)
    torch.save(out, path)
    return out
```

It memoises model outputs to a `.cache/` folder on disk, keyed on a hash of the input text. Next time the same inputs come through, it loads the saved output instead of re-running the model — useful when you're iterating on bucket edges or report formatting and don't want to pay for a fresh forward pass every time.

Whether to keep it is your call — that's a decision for you, not something I'll weigh in on.
